record.paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
record.original_question: For first-order phase transitions in compressed solids, discrepancies between phase-transition pressures predicted by the SK theory and experimentally measured pressures are reported to depend on both the material and the pressure range. If the theory is applied to a broader set of materials with known first-order phase-transition pressures, do systematic trends emerge in these discrepancies, and can such trends be characterized empirically well enough to reveal where the theory succeeds and where it fails?

evidence.quote: At first it would be useful to apply the theory to more materials for which first order phase transition presssures are known.In this way one would obtain a more precise empirical estimate of the systematic trends (if there are any) in the discrepancies between the calculated and measured values of the phase transition pressure.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the semiclassical Kirzhnits-type (SK) theory of dense matter, in which the total energy of a compressed solid is computed from a semiclassical density functional that includes Thomas–Fermi kinetic energy plus gradient (Kirzhnits) corrections, together with exchange and correlation contributions, evaluated on self-consistent electron densities. For a solid that undergoes a first-order structural phase transition between two crystal phases, the SK theory predicts a transition pressure p_SK as the pressure at which the Gibbs free energies (at zero temperature) of the two phases become equal. Let p_exp denote the experimentally measured transition pressure for the same material, and define the discrepancy Δ(M, p) = p_SK(M) − p_exp(M) as a function of the material M and the pressure range p in which the transition occurs.

Problem: Carry out the SK calculation for a broad collection of elemental and compound solids whose first-order phase-transition pressures are experimentally known, and determine whether the discrepancies Δ(M, p) exhibit systematic empirical trends as functions of: (i) the atomic number or mean atomic number of the constituents, (ii) the magnitude of the transition pressure, and (iii) the nature of the phases involved (e.g., metallic vs. insulating, close-packed vs. open structures). Characterize any such trends quantitatively (for instance, by fitting an empirical correction Δ ≈ f(Z, p, …)) precisely enough to delineate regimes in which the SK theory accurately predicts transition pressures from regimes in which it systematically fails.
artifact.status_search_result: No targeted follow-up study systematically benchmarking the SK semiclassical theory of dense matter across a wide range of first-order phase-transition materials could be located in the available literature. The question is posed as an open empirical research direction and its status remains undetermined.
